1 You, Tityrus, 'neath a broad beech-canopy 2 reclining, on the slender oat rehearse 3 your silvan ditties: I from my sweet fields, 4 and home's familiar bounds, even now depart. 5 Exiled from home am I; while, Tityrus, you 6 sit careless in the shade, and, at your call, 7 “Fair Amaryllis” bid the woods resound. 8 O Meliboeus, 'twas a god vouchsafed 9 this ease to us, for him a god will I 10 deem ever, and from my folds a tender lamb 11 oft with its life-blood shall his altar stain. 12 His gift it is that, as your eyes may see, 13 my kine may roam at large, and I myself 14 play on my shepherd's pipe what songs I will. 15 I grudge you not the boon, but marvel more, 16 such wide confusion fills the country-side. 17 See, sick at heart I drive my she-goats on, 18 and this one, O my Tityrus, scarce can lead: 19 for 'mid the hazel-thicket here but now 20 she dropped her new-yeaned twins on the bare flint, 21 hope of the flock—an ill, I mind me well, 22 which many a time, but for my blinded sense, 23 the thunder-stricken oak foretold, oft too 24 from hollow trunk the raven's ominous cry. 25 But who this god of yours? 1 the shepherd Corydon with love was fired 2 for fair Alexis, his own master's joy: 3 no room for hope had he, yet, none the less, 4 the thick-leaved shadowy-soaring beech-tree grove 5 still would he haunt, and there alone, as thus, 6 to woods and hills pour forth his artless strains. 7 “Cruel Alexis, heed you naught my songs? 8 Have you no pity? you'll drive me to my death. 9 Now even the cattle court the cooling shade 10 and the green lizard hides him in the thorn: 11 now for tired mowers, with the fierce heat spent, 12 pounds Thestilis her mess of savoury herbs, 13 wild thyme and garlic. I, with none beside, 14 save hoarse cicalas shrilling through the brake, 15 still track your footprints 'neath the broiling sun. 16 Better have borne the petulant proud disdain 17 of Amaryllis, or Menalcas wooed, 18 albeit he was so dark, and you so fair! 19 Trust not too much to colour, beauteous boy; 20 white privets fall, dark hyacinths are culled. 21 You scorn me, Alexis, who or what I am 22 care not to ask—how rich in flocks, or how 23 in snow-white milk abounding: yet for me 24 roam on Sicilian hills a thousand lambs; 25 summer or winter, still my milk-pails brim. 26 I sing as erst Amphion of Circe sang, 27 what time he went to call his cattle home 28 on Attic Aracynthus. 61 quinces all silvered-o'er with hoary down, 62 chestnuts, which Amaryllis wont to love, 63 and waxen plums withal: this fruit no less 64 shall have its meed of honour; and I will pluck 65 you too, ye laurels, and you, ye myrtles, near, 66 for so your sweets ye mingle. Corydon, 67 you are a boor, nor heeds a whit your gifts 68 alexis; no, nor would Iollas yield, 69 should gifts decide the day. Alack! alack! 70 What misery have I brought upon my head!— 71 loosed on the flowers Siroces to my bane, 72 and the wild boar upon my crystal springs! 73 Whom do you fly, infatuate? gods ere now, 74 and Dardan Paris, have made the woods their home. 75 Let Pallas keep the towers her hand hath built, 76 us before all things let the woods delight. 77 The grim-eyed lioness pursues the wolf, 78 the wolf the she-goat, the she-goat herself 79 in wanton sport the flowering cytisus, 80 and Corydon Alexis, each led on 81 by their own longing. See, the ox comes home 82 with plough up-tilted, and the shadows grow 83 to twice their length with the departing sun, 84 yet me love burns, for who can limit love? 85 Ah! Corydon, Corydon, what hath crazed your wit? 86 Your vine half-pruned hangs on the leafy elm; 87 why haste you not to weave what need requires 88 of pliant rush or osier? Scorned by this, 89 elsewhere some new Alexis you will find.”
